name: Brihadisvara Temple
traditions: Part of the 'Great Living Chola Temples' UNESCO group
significance: Dedicated to Shiva and also known as Rajarajesvaram, this is one of the largest Hindu temples in India and a defining example of mature Dravidian architecture.
story: The temple's vimana (tower) rises about 66 metres, built from granite hauled from quarries far from Thanjavur, and was completed in just seven years under Rajaraja I's administration.
legend: Local tradition holds that the temple's giant capstone was hauled up a specially built earthen ramp several kilometres long, though the exact engineering method is still debated by historians.
heritageStatus: UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1987, extended 2004 as part of the Great Living Chola Temples)

name: Kailasa Temple
patron: Commissioned during the reign of Krishna I
period: c. 8th century CE (dating debated among scholars)
traditions: Part of the Ellora Caves complex, shared by Hindu, Buddhist and Jain monuments
significance: Carved from a single rock face downward rather than built up, it is considered one of the most remarkable rock-cut structures in the world.
story: Unlike constructed temples, Kailasa was excavated top-down out of solid volcanic rock, with sculptors removing an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone to reveal the temple form within.
legend: Some oral traditions attribute the temple's inspiration to a king's vow to build a temple as tall as Mount Kailasa, Shiva's mythical abode, if his queen recovered from illness; this is a devotional legend rather than a documented historical event.
heritageStatus: Part of the Ellora Caves UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1983)

name: Shore Temple
patron: Attributed to the reign of Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)
traditions: Part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
significance: One of the earliest surviving structural (built, rather than rock-cut) stone temples in South India, marking a turning point from rock-cut to free-standing temple architecture.
story: Built facing the Bay of Bengal, the temple has endured centuries of sea wind and salt erosion, and its weathered carvings are still visible today.
legend: Local legend speaks of a group of 'Seven Pagodas' at Mahabalipuram, with six said to have been submerged by the sea; this remains a popular story rather than confirmed archaeological fact, though some underwater structures have been surveyed nearby.
heritageStatus: Part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1984)

name: Virupaksha Temple
patron: Commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi, consort of Vikramaditya II
traditions: Continues as an active place of worship today
significance: Considered the finest and largest of the temple cluster at Pattadakal, built to commemorate a Chalukya military victory over the Pallavas.
story: The temple was reportedly modeled on Pallava temples in Kanchipuram, reflecting the close artistic exchange, and rivalry, between the Chalukyas and Pallavas.
heritageStatus: Part of the Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1987)

name: Chennakeshava Temple
traditions: Continues as an active Vaishnava place of worship
significance: One of the finest examples of Hoysala temple architecture, celebrated for the density and precision of its stone carving.
story: Tradition holds construction took over 100 years and multiple generations of the Hoysala dynasty to complete, reflecting the scale of ambition behind the project.
heritageStatus: On UNESCO's World Heritage tentative list as part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas

name: Vittala Temple
patron: Associated with the reign of Krishnadeva Raya, with later additions
traditions: Hampi Utsav cultural festival held nearby
significance: Famous for its stone chariot and musical pillars, it represents Vijayanagara temple architecture at its most elaborate.
story: The temple's stone chariot, a shrine carved to resemble a wheeled temple cart, is one of the most recognized monuments in Hampi and appears on the Indian twenty-rupee note.
legend: Some of the temple's pillars are said to produce musical notes when tapped; this acoustic property is real and has been observed by visitors and researchers, though the full physical explanation is still studied.
heritageStatus: Part of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1986)
